name: Ifá / Òrìṣà tradition (Yoruba)

dating.dating_summary: Ifè was a functioning urban/religious center by 1200-1400 CE and the tradition's own oral corpus (Odù Ifá) locates origin there, but no archaeological find has been named-scholar-confirmed as Ifá divination practice specifically; the earliest substantive written attestation is mid-19th-century missionary/ethnographic (Crowther 1843; Ellis 1894; Johnson 1897/1921); the corpus itself is fundamentally oral, first systematically transcribed by Bascom (1950-51 fieldwork) and Abimbola (from the 1960s-70s) — treat pre-19th-century dating as genuinely open, not a settled figure.

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: Ilé-Ifè classical period (naturalistic bronze/terracotta art) dated c. 1200-1400 CE (Met Museum); no named excavation report ties a specific dated artifact to Ifá divination practice specifically.

earliest_written_attestation.note: Samuel Ajayi Crowther, A Vocabulary of the Yoruba Language (London, 1843; expanded ed. with Owen Vidal, 1852) is the earliest identified substantive written source; no confirmed pre-19th-century European account of Ifá/Òrìṣà worship specifically was located.

surviving_manuscript_date.note: No manuscript tradition; oral corpus first systematically transcribed by William Bascom (fieldwork 1950-51) and Wande Abimbola (Ifá Divination Poetry, NOK, 1977).

tradition_internal_claim.note: Odù Ifá locates origin at Ilé-Ifè, associated with Ọ̀rúnmìlà; some strands treat him as a primordial divinity, others as a historicized founding figure — internally contested within the tradition itself.

notes: Named scholars: Wande Abimbola (Ifá Divination Poetry, NOK 1977) and William Bascom (Ifa Divination: Communication Between Gods and Men in West Africa, Indiana UP, 1969/1991) — the two standard 20th-century academic authorities, both working from live oral recitation.
